children.text: Key Takeaways
Liability typically points to the driver who did not yield the right-of-way.
Colorado permits divided fault, adjusting compensation based on each party’s share of responsibility.
These collisions most often trace back to ignored signals, improper turns, or failure to yield.
Police reports and witness accounts are often central to establishing what happened.
Drivers are required to stay at the scene, swap information, and document the crash without delay.
When a
T-boned car accident

happens, determining fault is rarely as straightforward as it seems. Witness accounts conflict, traffic signals get disputed, and the full sequence of events takes careful reconstruction. Under Colorado law, how responsibility gets assigned has a direct impact on what an injured driver can recover, making a thorough review of the evidence the foundation of any serious claim.

In most cases, fault points to the driver who failed to yield, though Colorado’s comparative negligence framework allows both parties to carry a share of responsibility. Understanding how fault gets established and which evidence carries weight is where protecting a claim begins. At
Dormer Harpring
, our
car accident lawyers
approach each case with a thorough understanding of Colorado law and a careful review of the evidence that determines how a claim unfolds.
How T-Bone Accidents Happen
A
T-boned car accident

often occurs when one vehicle enters an intersection without the right-of-way and strikes another on the side. Whether the cause is a misjudged gap in traffic, an ignored signal, or a failure to check for oncoming vehicles, the result is a collision that leaves little room for evasive action. In Denver, heavy traffic and multi-lane crossings raise the risk considerably, particularly during peak commute hours when intersections see the highest volume of vehicles.
Most of these crashes trace back to a failure to respect the right-of-way:
Running a red light or stop sign
Making an unsafe left turn across traffic
Failing to yield during a right turn
Distracted or impaired driving
Speeding through intersections
When impact leaves no time to react, the legal question shifts to which driver had the right-of-way at the moment of the collision and whether any contributing factors were shared in the outcome.
Common Injuries from T-Bone Accidents

The mechanics of a side-impact crash make injuries particularly serious. Unlike the front or rear of a vehicle, the sides offer far less structural protection, meaning passengers absorb much of the force directly. Even with modern safety features, these collisions can produce trauma not immediately apparent at the scene but worsening significantly in the days following the crash.
Common injuries may include:
Traumatic brain injuries
caused by sudden head movement
Rib fractures and internal organ damage
Spinal cord injuries leading to long-term impairment
Pelvic and hip fractures from side intrusion
Soft tissue injuries affecting mobility and recovery

Many of these injuries do not show their full severity right away, even when treatment begins at the scene. The window between the crash and a proper diagnosis can quietly work against a claim, influencing both its value and how
pain and suffering
gets calculated in a final settlement. Consistent medical care and thorough documentation from the beginning go a long way toward keeping a claim intact.
Potentially Liable Parties in a T-Bone Accident

Side-impact crashes are not always the result of a single driver’s mistake. Depending on the circumstances, responsibility may fall on the driver who failed to yield or obey traffic signals, a second driver whose speeding or distraction contributed to the collision, a vehicle manufacturer when a mechanical defect played a role, an employer if the at-fault driver was acting within the scope of their job, or a government entity responsible for unsafe road design or signal failure.
Colorado’s modified comparative negligence system allows liability to be divided among multiple parties. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 13-21-111

, an injured party may recover damages as long as their share of fault stays below 50 percent, with compensation reduced proportionally. Insurers routinely attempt to shift blame to minimize payouts, making accurate fault analysis backed by traffic camera footage, witness statements, and police reports essential to any claim.
Steps to Take After a T-Bone Accident

Understanding who may be liable is only part of what determines how a claim unfolds. The decisions made in the minutes and hours following a crash are significant, and Colorado law establishes the minimum requirement for drivers to stay at the scene and exchange information. A few additional steps can make a considerable difference:
Seek medical attention, even when injuries seem minor
Call law enforcement to document the scene
Photograph vehicle positions, damage, and surroundings
Collect contact information from any witnesses
Notify your insurance provider promptly
Consult a car accident lawyer before providing detailed recorded statements

Physical evidence such as impact angle and vehicle placement can be decisive in establishing fault, yet it has a way of disappearing faster than most people anticipate. The sooner an injured driver begins documenting and preserving what happened, the stronger the foundation for any claim that follows.
Benefits of Legal Representation

When a claim is filed, insurance adjusters get to work quickly, and their priority is rarely paying full value. For injured drivers dealing with disputed fault or serious injuries, the difference between what is offered and what is actually owed can be considerable.

Closing that gap requires deliberate effort and a thorough understanding of Colorado law. Building a complete picture of the crash, engaging reconstruction experts, negotiating with carriers, and documenting every layer of damages, from immediate medical costs to long-term care and lost income, are all part of ensuring a claim reflects what an injured driver has genuinely been through.

In Colorado, how responsibility gets assigned can be just as consequential as the severity of the injuries themselves. Contesting an unfair fault determination is not a secondary concern; it is often central to recovering what an injured driver truly deserves.
